overview.text: Helen Adams Keller (1880–1968) was born in Tuscumbia, Alabama, and became deafblind after an illness at 19 months; the illness remains unidentified. In 1887, teacher Anne Sullivan began teaching her by spelling words into her hand, opening a path to communication and formal education. Keller attended Radcliffe College and graduated in 1904, the first deafblind person to earn a college degree. She published The Story of My Life in 1903, wrote many other works, and became a prominent advocate for people with disabilities, women’s suffrage, and workers’ rights. Her significance lies in both her literary career and decades of public advocacy for greater opportunity and access.

key_facts.text: On April 5, 1887, Sullivan fingerspelled “W-A-T-E-R” into Keller’s hand as water flowed over it; Keller connected the word with what she felt.
Keller graduated cum laude from Radcliffe in 1904, becoming the first deafblind person to earn a college degree.
Her autobiography, The Story of My Life, was published in 1903, while she was a student at Radcliffe.
Keller was a committed socialist, supported women’s suffrage, and became an early member of the American Civil Liberties Union.
From 1924, she worked as a public spokesperson for the American Foundation for the Blind, advocating for people with vision loss.
